questions_and_answers.question: What suffixes are used in German to form the comparative and superlative of adjectives and adverbs?
Which of the following pairs shows an umlaut change in the comparative?
What is the correct superlative phrase for 'Dieses Haus ist klein'?
Which irregular comparison set is correctly matched?
How does German express a complete comparison indicating 'not as ... as'?

answers.answer: Using 'nicht so' plus positive form and a phrase introduced by 'wie'

questions_and_answers.question: Which sentence correctly illustrates a comparison using a genitive phrase or prepositional phrase with a superlative?

answers.answer: Die Zugspitze ist der höchste Berg Deutschlands
Der Herbst ist wärmer als hier
Hier ist weniger Verkehr als im Tal
Heute ist es nicht so kalt wie gestern

questions_and_answers.question: Which of the following adjectives does NOT undergo an umlaut in its comparative form?
In the example 'Ich trinke lieber diesen Wein als den französischen', what is being compared?
Which sentence correctly repeats the preposition when making a comparison?

answers.answer: Sie kommen schneller mit dem Auto als mit der Strassenbahn in die Stadt
Der Vater ist älter als sein Sohn
Heute ist es nicht so kalt wie gestern

questions_and_answers.question: Which English words correspond to the German positive, comparative and superlative forms of 'schnell'?

articles.text:
Three different degrees of intensity are expressed by adjectives and adverbs. We noted this in Unit 4, where the adverbs gern, lieber and am liebsten were discussed. The same difference in degree is shown by a number of adjective and adverb forms occurring in the present unit:
Es ist nicht so kalt wie gestern.
Jetzt können wir schneller fahren.
Welche Jahreszeit ist am schönsten?
It's not as cold as yesterday.
Now we can go faster.
What season is the nicest one?

Positive, Comparative and Superlative forms

The forms of adjectives and adverbs corresponding to the different degrees of intensity are called POSITIVE, COMPARATIVE and SUPERLATIVE. Note the similarity of German and English forms:

Positive: kalt — cold, schnell — fast, schön — nice
Comparative: kälter — colder, schneller — faster, schöner — nicer
Superlative: kältest — coldest, schnellst — fastest, schönst — nicest

The suffixes -er and -est (or -st) are added to the basic, or positive form of the adjective or adverb to make the comparative and superlative. In addition to this monosyllabic German adjectives and adverbs change or ‘umlaut’ their stem vowels in the comparative and superlative forms. Relatively few adjectives and adverbs have umlaut in their comparative and superlative forms, but those which are umlauted are of rather frequent occurrence. Here is a list of adjectives and adverbs encountered up to this point in which umlaut takes place (some show other irregularities which will be pointed out later): alt, gross, hoch, kurz, lang, nah, oft, warm.

English also uses the words ‘more’ and ‘most’ to indicate comparative and superlative degree, especially with words of several syllables. German however uses only the suffixes. For example: praktisch – praktischer – praktischst (practical – more practical – most practical), umständlich – umständlicher – umständlichst (complicated – more complicated – most complicated). The superlative suffix is usually –st, but it is –est after s (heissest), t (kältest) or z (kürzest). It may be either –st or –est after vowels (neust, neuest).

Stem‑lengtheners versus endings

The comparative and superlative suffixes are not endings. They are stem‑lengtheners, to which endings are added when the comparative and superlative forms occur as attributive adjectives, i.e. as part of an adjective–noun or specifier–adjective–noun phrase:
Die Zugspitze ist der höchste Berg Deutschlands. – The Zugspitze is the highest mountain in Germany.
Ich habe einen dickeren Pullover an. – I have a heavier sweater on.
Das ist ein schwerer Wagen. – That is a heavy car.
Das ist ein schwererer Wagen. – That is a heavier car.
Das ist unser neuer Teppich. – That is our new rug.
Das ist unser neuster Teppich. – That is our newest rug.
Hier ist eine teure Lampe. – Here is an expensive lamp.
Hier ist eine teurere Lampe. – Here is a more expensive lamp.

Predicate adjectives and adverbs

Positive and comparative forms occurring as predicate adjectives or adverbs have no endings. Superlative forms, however, occur in a special predicate phrase:
Dieses Haus ist klein. – This house is small.
Dieses Haus ist kleiner. – This house is smaller.
Dieses Haus ist am kleinsten. – This house is the smallest.
Dieses Haus ist das kleinste Haus von allen. – This house is the smallest house of all.
Unser Wagen fährt schnell. – Our car is going fast.
Unser Wagen fährt schneller. – Our car is going faster.
Unser Wagen fährt am schnellsten. – Our car is going fastest.

Irregular comparison

A few adjectives and adverbs are quite irregular in their comparative and superlative formation. The following is a list of those encountered up to this point:

gern – lieber – liebst (gladly, more gladly, most gladly)
gross – grösser – grösst (large, larger, largest)
gut – besser – best (good, better, best)
hoch – höher – höchst (high, higher, highest)
nah – näher – nächst (near, nearer, nearest)
viel – mehr – meist (much, more, most)

Complete comparison

A complete comparison may contain a comparative form of the adjective or adverb and a phrase introduced by als (“than”), or, in the negative, nicht so plus the positive form of the adjective or adverb and a phrase introduced by wie (“as”):
Der Herbst ist länger und wärmer als hier. – The fall is longer and warmer than it is here.
Heute ist es nicht so kalt wie gestern. – Today it's not as cold as yesterday.
Hier ist weniger Verkehr als unten im Tal. – There's less traffic here than down in the valley.
Hier ist nicht so viel Verkehr wie unten im Tal. – There's not as much traffic here as down in the valley.
Der Vater ist natürlich älter als sein Sohn. – The father is naturally older than his son.
Der Sohn ist nicht so alt wie sein Vater. – The son is not as old as his father.
Ich trinke lieber diesen Wein als den französischen. – I prefer to drink this wine rather than the French one.
Sie kommen schneller mit dem Auto als mit der Strassenbahn in die Stadt. – They come faster into town by car than by streetcar. Note that phrases following als and wie have the same case forms as the phrases with which they are being compared and prepositions are repeated.

A complete comparison may also contain a superlative form plus a genitive form or a phrase introduced by the prepositions in or von:
Die Zugspitze ist der höchste Berg Deutschlands. – The Zugspitze is the highest mountain in Germany (Germany's highest mountain).
Der Everest ist der höchste Berg in der ganzen Welt. – Everest is the highest mountain in the whole world.
Von allen Städten Amerikas hat Washington das heisseste und feuchteste Wetter in den Sommermonaten. – Of all the cities in America Washington has the hottest and most humid weather in the summer months.
